clue.text: Lungs Adam trained before start of individual medley

indicators.note: the rearranged letters come before the next piece in the answer
letters that are trained are drilled into a new shape, so these two words are rearranged
only the opening letter of the following word is used

explanation.surface: A swimming coach has Adam's lungs trained ahead of the individual medley race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Individual medley' reads as a swimming event, but 'medley' alone is the definition. Rearranging LUNGS ADAM gives SALMAGUND, and 'start of' takes I from 'individual'.
explanation.definitionFit: A salmagundi is a mixed salad dish, and by extension any miscellaneous mixture or assortment.

clue.text: Very angry squire fully absorbed

indicators.note: something absorbed is soaked up inside, so the answer sits inside the run of letters across these two words

explanation.surface: A country squire, totally engrossed, is livid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'absorbed' looks like it describes the squire's state of mind, but it signals that the answer lies within 'squIRE FULly'.
explanation.definitionFit: Ireful is a literary adjective built on ire, wrath, so it describes someone full of rage.

clue.text: New rising-generation politician expressing denial

indicators.note: in a down clue, rising means the word is read upwards, so backwards

parts.note: an age is a generation or era
a Tory is a member of the UK Conservative Party

explanation.surface: A new politician from the rising generation is busy issuing denials.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rising' turns AGE upside down in this down clue to give EGA. NEGATORY is American radio jargon for 'no'.
explanation.definitionFit: Negatory is a jokey, originally US radio-operator word meaning negative, a way of saying no.

clue.text: 'We're doomed!' Mainwaring — at last, Fraser finally opens drinks

indicators.note: only the closing letter of the preceding name is used
the letter opens up the drinks by going inside them

parts.note: ones are drinks, as in 'one for the road'

indicators.note: only the closing letter of the preceding name is used

explanation.surface: In Dad's Army Private Fraser wails 'We're doomed!' to Captain Mainwaring as drinks are opened.
explanation.walkthrough: Dad's Army is a classic British TV sitcom about the wartime Home Guard; Captain Mainwaring leads it and Private Fraser's catchphrase is 'We're doomed!'. G from 'at last' and R from 'finally' are placed around and inside ONES.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying we are doomed is saying we are goners, people beyond rescue, as a colloquial exclamation.

clue.text: Diner eating a source of rocket?

indicators.note: the outer word eats the next piece, taking it inside

parts.note: a luncher is someone eating a midday meal, a diner

explanation.surface: A restaurant customer eating rocket salad asks where it came from.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rocket' looks like the salad leaf a diner eats, but the definition is a rocket launcher, the thing a rocket comes from; the question mark flags the trick.
explanation.definitionFit: A launcher fires rockets or missiles, so it is literally where a rocket sets off from.

clue.text: Wow! Red Guard oddly dismissed

indicators.note: the letters in odd positions are thrown out, leaving only the even-placed ones

explanation.surface: An exclamation of surprise as a Red Guard is strangely sacked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'oddly dismissed' removes letters 1, 3, 5 and 7 of 'Red Guard', keeping E, G, A and D.
explanation.definitionFit: Egad is an old-fashioned mild oath expressing surprise, like gosh or wow.

clue.text: Run into husband with wife that is plain

indicators.note: the run abbreviation goes into the couple

parts.note: a husband with his wife make a pair
R is the cricket abbreviation for run
i.e. abbreviates id est, Latin for that is

explanation.surface: A husband and wife bump into each other on a flat, open expanse.
explanation.definitionFit: A prairie is a large open grassland in North America, a type of plain.

clue.text: Pleb chatted freely about it in fierce set-to

indicators.note: the rearranged letters wrap around the following word
chatting freely means the words run loose, so their letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A commoner talks openly about a fierce brawl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'freely' rearranges the first two words into PCHEDBATTLE, and 'about' wraps those letters around the plain 'it'.
explanation.definitionFit: A pitched battle is a planned full-scale engagement, and figuratively any intense, bitter clash.

clue.text: Oscar classifies trees

parts.note: Oscar is O in the NATO phonetic alphabet
to range things is to arrange or class them in order

explanation.surface: Oscar sorts woodland into categories.
explanation.definitionFit: Orange trees bear the citrus fruit, and the bare plural names the trees as well as the fruit.

clue.text: Extremely smart guide backing number one by council worker?

indicators.note: only the extreme letters at each end of the word are taken
backing means going in reverse, so this word is read backwards

parts.note: to steer is to guide
number one is a childish euphemism for urinating, a wee
per means by, as in per post

explanation.surface: A smart guide reverses behind someone in council employment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backing' turns STEER into REETS. A street sweeper is a typical council employee, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Street cleaning is a local-authority service, so a street sweeper is a classic example of someone a council employs.

clue.text: Issue over plan in which event should occur

indicators.note: over means turned over, so this word is read backwards

parts.note: to emit is to issue or send out
a frame is a framework or plan

explanation.surface: Someone raises a point about the schedule for an event.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' turns EMIT into TIME. The definition is a descriptive phrase for the period during which something is scheduled.
explanation.definitionFit: A timeframe is the period of time within which something is planned to happen.

clue.text: Unlimited trading hit rock bottom

indicators.note: hit is read as stricken or knocked about, so the letters are jumbled
without its limits, the word loses its first and last letters

explanation.surface: Unrestricted trading on the markets crashed to its lowest point.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unlimited' strips the ends of 'trading' to leave RADIN, and 'hit' rearranges that.
explanation.definitionFit: The nadir is the lowest point of anything, so it is a synonym of rock bottom.

clue.text: Philosopher once a good-hearted cad

indicators.note: the letter forms the heart of the other word, going into its middle

parts.note: a heel is a cad, a dishonourable man

explanation.surface: A thinker of old was a kindly rogue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'good-hearted' reads as kind, but splits into G placed at the heart of HEEL.
explanation.definitionFit: Georg Hegel was a German idealist philosopher who died in 1831, hence 'once'.

clue.text: Old architectural engineers initially adopting small imperial measurements for heating facility

indicators.note: the initials take in the other pieces, adopting them inside
only the first letter of each of the three words is used

parts.note: a thou is a thousandth of an inch, an imperial measurement

explanation.surface: Old architects and engineers take on small imperial units for a heating plant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'initially' gives OAE, and 'adopting' places S THOUS between the A and E.
explanation.definitionFit: An oast house is a building with a kiln for drying hops by heating them, typical of Kent in England.

clue.text: One capturing potentially first class likeness

indicators.note: the outer word captures the inner piece, holding it inside

parts.note: unity is oneness, being one
Form I is the first class in some schools, so a pupil there might be potentially in the first class

explanation.surface: A single thing may well capture first-class similarity.
explanation.walkthrough: Form I is the first-year class in some British schools, which a new pupil is potentially in.
explanation.definitionFit: Uniformity is sameness, everything being alike, which is likeness taken broadly.

clue.text: Dirty, gutless, threatening regime

indicators.note: with its innards removed, only the outer letters of the word stay

parts.note: nasty can mean menacing or threatening

explanation.surface: A grubby, cowardly and menacing government.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gutless' looks like a slur on the regime but strips 'Dirty' to DY.
explanation.definitionFit: A dynasty is a line of hereditary rulers, a ruling family and therefore a form of regime.

clue.text: Praise fourth man guarding garrison

indicators.note: the outer word guards the inner piece by surrounding it

parts.note: in Genesis Seth is the fourth man, after Adam, Cain and Abel
a fort is a garrison

explanation.surface: Someone praises the fourth man on duty guarding the fort.
explanation.walkthrough: SET FORTH in an old sense means to praise or commend, though today it usually means to state or to depart.
explanation.definitionFit: Chambers lists an archaic sense of set forth as to commend or extol, so it is a synonym of praise.

clue.text: Third person singular I utter about first

indicators.note: the jumbled letters come first, before the abbreviation
about means scattered around, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: S is the grammatical abbreviation for singular

explanation.surface: A grammar lesson on the third person singular as I speak about it first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Third person singular' looks like grammar, but 'Third person' is the definition: TERTIUS was the label for the third boy of a surname at a British public school.
explanation.definitionFit: Tertius is Latin for third, used in old British schools for the third pupil sharing a surname.

clue.text: Film Martin and Robin et al

definitions.meaning: the martin and the robin are birds

explanation.surface: A film starring Martin and Robin and others.
explanation.walkthrough: Martin and Robin look like actors' names in a cast list, but they are species of bird.
explanation.definitionFit: Martins and robins are kinds of bird, and the Hitchcock movie bears the same name.

clue.text: Patrician talker regularly a pupil of Plato

parts.note: an aristo, short for aristocrat, is a patrician

indicators.note: taking letters at regular intervals, every other one from the word

explanation.surface: A posh speaker regularly sat at Plato's feet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly' picks T, L and E from 'talker'.
explanation.definitionFit: Aristotle studied at Plato's Academy in Athens for some twenty years before founding his own school.

clue.text: Brood about hard faith lessons in Jewish period

indicators.note: about here means turned about, so this word is read backwards

parts.note: to sit on eggs is to brood them
H is the pencil-grading abbreviation for hard
RI is religious instruction, school lessons in faith

explanation.surface: Brooding about tough religious education during a Jewish season.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' reverses the word for brood. Religious instruction was the old British school subject name.
explanation.definitionFit: Tishri is the seventh month of the Jewish calendar, falling in September and October.

clue.text: Crowd travelled by car

definitions.meaning: a large moving crowd, of animals or people
the past tense of drive, to travel by car

explanation.definitionFit: A drove is a herd or throng, and drove is also the past tense of drive.

clue.text: Two little animals raised another

indicators.note: in a down clue, raised means lifted upwards, so read from the bottom

parts.note: two kids, young goats, written one after the other

explanation.surface: Two young creatures brought up another one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Two' doubles KID, and 'raised' reads KIDKID upwards; 'another' means another little animal.
explanation.definitionFit: A dik-dik is a tiny African antelope, so it is one more small animal after the kids.

clue.text: Forbidden flutter about horses, two in 2nd and 3rd places

indicators.note: about means turned around, so this word is read backwards

parts.note: to bat your eyelids is to flutter them

indicators.note: the second letter of the word is taken
the third letter of the word is taken

explanation.surface: A forbidden bet on horses, two of them placed second and third.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flutter' and 'horses' suggest a bet on a race, but flutter means bat, as eyelids; 'about' reverses it to TAB. Then O is second in 'horses' and O third in 'two'.
explanation.definitionFit: Taboo describes something banned by custom or social prohibition.

clue.text: Made move, swapping sides in plot

indicators.note: left side is exchanged for the right side, one abbreviation for the other

parts.note: blew means moved by air, as the wind blew

explanation.surface: Someone moved, changing sides in a conspiracy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'swapping sides' changes L (left) for R (right).
explanation.definitionFit: To brew trouble is to plot or hatch it, as in 'something is brewing'.

clue.text: Bank statement initiating planned cash withdrawal?

definitions.text: Bank statement initiating planned cash withdrawal?

parts.words: Bank statement initiating planned cash withdrawal?
parts.note: a bank robber's command at the start of a raid, a bank statement in a new sense

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bank statement' suggests a monthly account summary; here it is something said in a bank by an armed robber.
explanation.definitionFit: A robber orders the staff to raise their hands before taking the money, an unauthorised withdrawal.

clue.text: One puts up English clergyman

parts.note: a rector is a parish clergyman

explanation.surface: An English vicar plays host to someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'puts up' suggests giving a guest a bed, but an erector puts up structures.
explanation.definitionFit: An erector is someone who erects, builds or raises things upright.

clue.text: Paper getting more sarcastic about Rolling Stone

indicators.note: the outer word goes about the paper, surrounding it

parts.note: drier means more dry, drier humour being more sarcastic
the FT is the Financial Times newspaper

explanation.surface: A newspaper grows snarkier about the Rolling Stones.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rolling Stone' looks like the band, but it is the proverb 'a rolling stone gathers no moss', someone who keeps moving on.
explanation.definitionFit: A drifter wanders from place to place without settling, like the proverbial rolling stone.
